The '''European Centre for the Development of Professional Training''' ('''Cedefop''') is an [[agency of the European Union|agency]] of the [[European Union]]. The Agency was established in 1975. Cedefop is headquartered and located in [[Thessaloniki (regional unit)|Thessaloniki Region]], [[Greece]], and has a [[Brussels]] office. Cedefop is the [[acronym]] of its French title, '''<u>C</u>entre <u>E</u>uropéen pour le <u>Dé</u>veloppement de la <u>Fo</u>rmation <u>P</u>rofessionnelle''' ('''C.E.DE.FO.P.'''). Cedefop supports the development of European [[professional education]] policies and contributes to their implementation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professional excellence {{!}} ETF |url=https://www.etf.europa.eu/en/what-we-do/professional-excellence |access-date=2023-05-14 |website=www.etf.europa.eu}}</ref>

Cedefop works closely with the [[European Commission]], [[government]]s, representatives of [[employer]]s and [[trade union]]s, [[Research|researchers]] and practitioners in professional education, with the aim of strengthening European cooperation. It provides the evidence on which to base European professional education policy and identifies trends in and challenges for professional education. The agency also brings together policy-makers, social partners, researchers and practitioners to share ideas and debate the best ways to improve European professional education policies. The issues it covers span guidance and counselling; training for older workers; forecasting the demand and supply of [[skills]]; the recognition and validation of learning that takes place outside the education system; and the development of [[professional certification|qualification]] frameworks.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-11-28 |title=European investors set up N4.5b professional centre in Enugu to curb migration |url=https://guardian.ng/news/nigeria/european-investors-set-up-n4-5b-professional-centre-in-enugu-to-curb-migration/ |location=Lagos, Nigeria|access-date=2023-05-14 |newspaper=[[The Guardian (Nigeria)|The Guardian]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

The '''European Union Agency for Cybersecurity'''<ref name="enisa-euvd">{{cite web |title=Consult the European Vulnerability Database to enhance your digital security! |url=https://www.enisa.europa.eu/news/consult-the-european-vulnerability-database-to-enhance-your-digital-security |publisher=ENISA |date=13 May 2025 |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref> – self-designation '''ENISA''' from the abbreviation of its original name – is an [[agency of the European Union]]. It is fully operational since 1 September 2005. The Agency is located in [[Athens]], [[Greece]] and has offices in Brussels, Belgium and [[Heraklion]], Greece.            

ENISA was created in 2004 by EU Regulation No 460/2004<ref>{{CELEX|32004R0460|text=Regulation (EC) No 460/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 March 2004 establishing the European Network and Information Security Agency}}</ref> under the name of '''European Network and Information Security Agency'''. ENISA's Regulation is the EU Regulation No 2019/881<ref name="32019R0881">{{CELEX|32019R0881|text=Regulation (EU) 2019/881 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on ENISA (the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) and on information and communications technology cybersecurity certification and repealing Regulation (EU) No 526/2013 (Cybersecurity Act)}}</ref> of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on ENISA (the '''European Union Agency for Cybersecurity''') and on information and communications technology cybersecurity certification and repealing EU Regulation No 526/2013 (Cybersecurity Act).  

ENISA, is the Union’s agency dedicated to achieving a high common level of [[Computer security|cybersecurity]] across Europe. Established in 2004 and strengthened by the EU Cybersecurity Act, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity contributes to EU cyber policy, enhances the trustworthiness of ICT products, services and processes with cybersecurity certification schemes, cooperates with Member States and EU bodies, and helps Europe prepare for the cyber challenges of tomorrow. Through knowledge sharing, capacity building and awareness raising, the Agency works together with its key stakeholders to strengthen trust in the connected economy, to boost resilience of the Union’s infrastructure, and, ultimately, to keep Europe’s society and citizens digitally secure.
